# thoth

> Containerized agent environment: OpenCode + goose/goosetown + kubectl, with a Prometheus metrics endpoint, a generic skill pack, and Docker Compose wiring. Maintained and supported by jarakube.eu. This file is the complete documentation flattened for LLM consumption.

## File: README.md

![thoth](https://img.shields.io/badge/maintained%20by-jarakube.eu-blue)

Containerized OpenCode agent environment for Kubernetes and Ceph-focused
operations, with Goose/Goosetown multi-agent support and a built-in
Prometheus metrics endpoint for agent runs.

Named after [Thoth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thoth), the ancient
Egyptian deity of wisdom, writing, and knowledge.

### Project purpose

This repository builds a CLI agent image that combines:

- [OpenCode](https://opencode.ai) (`opencode-ai`) for interactive coding/ops workflows
- [Goose](https://github.com/aaif-goose/goose) + [Goosetown](https://github.com/aaif-goose/goosetown) for multi-agent orchestration
- `kubectl` for Kubernetes cluster access
- A small, generic skill pack (currently a Ceph expert skill)

The result is a ready-to-run agent container for infrastructure-heavy tasks
where Kubernetes and storage knowledge are needed in the same environment.

### Maintainer and support

This project is maintained and supported by
**[jarakube.eu](https://jarakube.eu)** - the sovereign Kubernetes platform
by [Jaraco GmbH](https://www.jaraco.de).

- Issues, feature requests, and contributions are welcome via GitHub.
- Commercial support, hosting, and platform integrations are available
  through jarakube.eu.
- The example MCP server used in the docs
  ([jarakube.eu/mcp](https://jarakube.eu/mcp)) is operated by the same
  platform.

### What the image contains

| Component | Location in container | Notes |
|-----------|----------------------|-------|
| OpenCode | `/usr/local/bin/opencode` | Installed from npm (`opencode-ai@latest`) by default; see below for custom builds |
| Goose | `/usr/local/bin/goose` | Pinned via `ARG GOOSE_VERSION` (default `v1.50.0`) |
| Goosetown | `/app/goosetown` | Public [aaif-goose/goosetown](https://github.com/aaif-goose/goosetown) git submodule |
| kubectl | `/usr/local/bin/kubectl` | v1.36 from pkgs.k8s.io |
| Skills | `/home/appuser/.config/opencode/skills/` | Everything from repo `skills/` directory |
| Metrics exporter | `/app/scripts/opencode-prometheus-exporter.py` | Listens on `:9464` |
| gh CLI | `/usr/bin/gh` | For GitHub workflows from inside the container |

#### Use a custom opencode build

By default the image installs the official `opencode-ai` release from npm. To
use your own opencode build (e.g. a patched fork):

1. Build the binary (see the [opencode repo](https://github.com/sst/opencode));
   for the Keycloak-enabled fork use
   [jaracogmbh/opencode, branch `feature/34733/keycloak-sso-token-expiry-issue`](https://github.com/jaracogmbh/opencode/tree/feature/34733/keycloak-sso-token-expiry-issue)
   (see [Configure OpenCode to use Keycloak](#configure-opencode-to-use-keycloak)):
   ```bash
   git clone --branch feature/34733/keycloak-sso-token-expiry-issue \
     https://github.com/jaracogmbh/opencode.git
   cd opencode
   bun install && bun run build --single
   ```
2. Place it at `build/opencode/opencode` in the repository root.
3. In the `Dockerfile`, comment the `npm install -g opencode-ai@latest` line
   and uncomment the `COPY build/opencode/opencode ...` line.
4. `docker build` as usual.

### Build and run

Build:

```bash
git clone --recurse-submodules <this-repo-url>
cd thoth
docker build -t thoth .
```

Run interactively:

```bash
docker run --rm -it thoth
```

#### Docker Compose (recommended)

The easiest way to run the container. User-generated data stays on the host
filesystem; only OpenCode auth/session state lives in a named volume:

```bash
cp .env.example .env   # optional: add provider keys, set WORKSPACE_DIR
make up                # = HOST_UID=$(id -u) HOST_GID=$(id -g) docker compose up -d --build
make shell             # interactive bash in /workspace
```

- The agent lands in `/workspace` (defaults to `./workspace/`, override with
  `WORKSPACE_DIR` in `.env`)
- All user-generated data stays on the **host filesystem**: workspace and
  per-run metrics (`./share/opencode-runs/`) are bind mounts you can inspect
  directly
- A **goosetown working clone** is created at `workspace/goosetown` on first
  start (host-visible), and all goosetown env (`GOOSETOWN_DIR`, `GUIDES_DIR`,
  `PLANS_DIR`, `RESEARCH_DIR`, `WORK_LOGS_DIR`) points into it. Override with
  `GOOSETOWN_DIR`/`GOOSETOWN_REPO_URL`/`GOOSETOWN_REF` to use your own fork
  or an existing clone
- `opencode auth login` state persists in the `opencode-data` named volume
  across restarts (kept out of the project dir since it holds credentials)
- Prometheus metrics at `http://localhost:9464/metrics`
- One-shot sessions: `make run CMD="opencode"` or
  `docker compose run --rm thoth opencode`

Permissions: the image builds `appuser` with your host uid/gid
(`APP_UID`/`APP_GID` build args; `make` passes them automatically, plain
`docker compose` reads `HOST_UID`/`HOST_GID` from `.env` or the
environment). Host bind-mount directories must exist and be writable by
that uid - the defaults ship `.gitkeep` files so they exist with your
ownership after clone. Nothing on the host is ever chowned by compose or
the container.

If you need cluster access, mount your kubeconfig (uncomment the line in
`docker-compose.yml`):

```yaml
volumes:
  - ${HOME}/.kube:/home/appuser/.kube:ro
```

With the metrics endpoint exposed (plain docker):

```bash
docker run --rm -it \
  -p 9464:9464 \
  -v "$(pwd):/app" \
  -v "$HOME/.local/share/opencode/auth.json:/home/appuser/.local/share/opencode/auth.json:ro" \
  thoth
```

Then scrape:

```bash
curl http://127.0.0.1:9464/metrics
```

### Per-run OpenCode metrics

Use `./scripts/opencode-run-with-metrics.sh` when you need session-scoped token
and cost reporting instead of global `opencode stats` output.

Example:

```bash
./scripts/opencode-run-with-metrics.sh \
  --metrics-dir share/opencode-runs \
  --title-prefix blogpost-ci \
  -- --model openai/gpt-5.4 "Reply with exactly OK"
```

The wrapper:

- creates a unique run title
- runs `opencode run --format json`
- captures the emitted `sessionID`
- exports that exact session with `opencode export`
- writes raw events, stderr logs, the exported session, and `run-metrics.json`
  under `share/opencode-runs/<run-title>/`

This avoids mixing usage across multiple sessions or projects and is a better
fit for CI reporting.

### Prometheus endpoint

The container starts a lightweight Prometheus exporter on `:9464` by default
and exposes `/metrics`.

The exporter reads the per-run artifacts under `share/opencode-runs/` and
publishes aggregated metrics such as:

- `opencode_runs_total`
- `opencode_run_duration_seconds_total`
- `opencode_tokens_total{token_kind=...}`
- `opencode_cost_usd_total`
- `opencode_messages_total{role=...}`
- `opencode_tool_calls_total{tool=...,status=...}`
- `opencode_step_finishes_total{reason=...}`
- `opencode_log_events_total{service=...,status=...,event_type=...}`
- `opencode_log_tool_failures_total{tool=...,kind=...}`
- `opencode_log_errors_total{kind=...}`

Configuration:

- `OPENCODE_METRICS_ENABLED=0` disables the exporter
- `OPENCODE_METRICS_HOST` sets the listen address
- `OPENCODE_METRICS_PORT` sets the listen port
- `OPENCODE_RUN_METRICS_DIR` sets the run artifact directory used by both the
  wrapper and exporter

Minimal Prometheus scrape config:

```yaml
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: thoth
    static_configs:
      - targets:
          - localhost:9464
```

### Skills

See [skills/README.md](skills/README.md) for the full documentation of the
skill system, including how to add your own skills and how to **map skills
into the container at runtime** (bind mount, volume, ConfigMap, PVC, derived
image, or git clone) instead of bundling them into the image.

Quick summary:

```bash
# development: mount host skills over the bundled ones
docker run --rm -it \
  -v "$(pwd)/my-skills:/home/appuser/.config/opencode/skills:ro" \
  thoth
```

### Goose / Goosetown

The image also ships [Goose](https://github.com/aaif-goose/goose) and the
[Goosetown](https://github.com/aaif-goose/goosetown) multi-agent framework:

```bash
# interactive goose session
goose session

# goosetown orchestrator (alias: gt)
goose load source:goosetown-orchestrator

# goose backed by a LiteLLM proxy
goose-litellm session "Analyze this codebase"
```

Details:

- [LITELLM_CONFIGURATION.md](LITELLM_CONFIGURATION.md) - configuring the
  agents against a LiteLLM proxy: goose via the `goose-litellm` wrapper,
  OpenCode via a custom `openai-compatible` provider (OpenCode has no
  native litellm provider - it connects to LiteLLM's OpenAI-compatible API)
- [GOOSETOWN_INTEGRATION.md](GOOSETOWN_INTEGRATION.md) - what the image sets
  up for goosetown (paths, wrappers, telepathy)
- `configure-goose.sh` - helper to drive `goose configure` non-interactively
  inside a running container (`CONTAINER=<name> ./configure-goose.sh`)

#### One config for both agents

OpenCode and goose need the same data to reach an LLM endpoint (URL, API
key, model list) but store it differently. `scripts/sync-llm-config.sh`
keeps them in sync from a **single source of truth** - the `LLM_*`
environment variables - and runs automatically at container start:

```bash
# .env - configure once, both agents follow
LLM_ENDPOINT=http://litellm-proxy:4000/v1   # includes /v1
LLM_MODELS=mistral-small-latest mistral-large-latest
CUSTOM_LITELLM_API_KEY=sk-...
```

```bash
# apply and verify
docker compose up -d
docker compose exec thoth opencode models litellm   # OpenCode: litellm/<model> entries
docker compose exec thoth goose doctor               # goose: "new session · litellm <model>"
```

The script writes the OpenCode custom provider config
(`~/.config/opencode/opencode.json`), the goose provider selection
(`~/.config/goose/config.yaml`, using goose's built-in `litellm`
provider), and the shared `LITELLM_*` env for goose sessions. Unset
`LLM_ENDPOINT` = no-op; each agent falls back to its own configuration.
After changing `LLM_*` in `.env`, restart with `docker compose up -d` to
re-run the sync. See [LITELLM_CONFIGURATION.md](LITELLM_CONFIGURATION.md)
for the full variable reference.

#### Keeping the API key out of .env (pass / compose secrets)

The key never needs to live in `.env` or the compose file. Three options:

1. **`pass` (recommended)** - store the key in the standard Unix password
   store and let `make up` wire it in:

   ```bash
   pass init <your-gpg-id>
   pass insert -m llm/thoth-api-key    # paste the key

   make up    # exports the key from pass into the llm_api_key compose secret
   ```

   The Makefile resolves `PASS_LLM_ENTRY` (default `llm/thoth-api-key`)
   into a temporary mode-600 file, mounts it as the `llm_api_key` docker
   compose secret, and deletes the file afterwards. Without pass or the
   entry, `make up` starts without the secret and falls back to `.env`.

2. **Compose secret via any secret manager** - point `LLM_API_KEY_FILE`
   in `.env` at a file containing the key (sops, vault, 1password CLI,
   plain file - your choice). The file is mounted read-only at
   `/run/secrets/llm_api_key`.

3. **Plain env var** - `CUSTOM_LITELLM_API_KEY` in `.env` (simplest, but
   visible in `docker inspect` and shell history).

In all cases the sync script reads the key from the env var or the
secret file and exports it for the agents - it is never written to any
generated config file (configs only reference the variable).

Goosetown runs as a **working clone inside the workspace**: the container
entrypoint clones `https://github.com/aaif-goose/goosetown.git` to
`workspace/goosetown` on first start (skipped if the directory already
exists), and points `GOOSETOWN_DIR`, `GUIDES_DIR`, `PLANS_DIR`,
`RESEARCH_DIR` and `WORK_LOGS_DIR` at it. Its working dirs live inside the
clone (upstream gitignores them), so everything the orchestrator produces
persists on the host through the workspace bind mount. Use your own fork via
`GOOSETOWN_REPO_URL`/`GOOSETOWN_REF`, or point `GOOSETOWN_DIR` at an existing
clone. The image also carries a tooling copy at `/app/goosetown` used as
fallback for the `goose` telepathy wrapper.

### CI

`.github/workflows/build.yml` builds the image on every push to `main`
and publishes it to `ghcr.io/<owner>/thoth` using the default
`GITHUB_TOKEN`. No private registries or secrets are required. Published
images are also scanned with Trivy (fail on CRITICAL/HIGH findings,
unfixed only); the scan runs on every push, not on pull requests.

### Configure OpenCode to use Keycloak

> **Note: this requires a custom OpenCode build.** The stock
> `opencode-ai` release installed by default (via npm) does not include
> the Keycloak authentication feature - `auth.keycloak` config and
> `opencode auth login keycloak` come from a patched OpenCode fork. The
> reference fork with the Keycloak patches is
> [jaracogmbh/opencode (branch `feature/34733/keycloak-sso-token-expiry-issue`)](https://github.com/jaracogmbh/opencode/tree/feature/34733/keycloak-sso-token-expiry-issue).
> Clone that branch, build the binary, and place it at
> `build/opencode/opencode` before building the image (see
> [Use a custom opencode build](#use-a-custom-opencode-build)); the
> Dockerfile then uses it instead of the npm release. With the stock
> npm release, this section does not apply.

OpenCode in this image supports a global Keycloak login plus MCP server
configs that reuse that bearer token.

1. Add Keycloak defaults to your OpenCode config.

   Use either a project config like `.opencode/opencode.jsonc` or a global
   config like `~/.config/opencode/opencode.jsonc`:

   ```jsonc
   {
     "auth": {
       "keycloak": {
         "issuer": "https://sso.example.com/realms/my-realm",
         "clientId": "opencode-cli",
         "scope": "openid profile email offline_access"
       }
     },
     "mcp": {
       "jira": {
         "type": "remote",
         "url": "https://mcp.example.com",
         "auth": {
           "type": "bearer",
           "provider": "keycloak"
         }
       }
     }
   }
   ```

   You can also provide the Keycloak defaults through environment variables:

   - `OPENCODE_KEYCLOAK_ISSUER`
   - `OPENCODE_KEYCLOAK_CLIENT_ID`
   - `OPENCODE_KEYCLOAK_CLIENT_SECRET`
   - `OPENCODE_KEYCLOAK_SCOPE`
   - `OPENCODE_KEYCLOAK_REDIRECT_URI`

2. Log into Keycloak once.

   ```bash
   opencode auth login keycloak
   ```

   This stores the session in `~/.local/share/opencode/auth.json`.

3. Reuse that login inside the container.

   The simplest workflow is to authenticate on the host, then mount the auth
   file into the container:

   ```bash
   docker run --rm -it \
     -v "$HOME/.local/share/opencode/auth.json:/home/appuser/.local/share/opencode/auth.json:ro" \
     -v "$HOME/.config/opencode:/home/appuser/.config/opencode:ro" \
     thoth
   ```

   This is the recommended path because the default Keycloak callback binds
   to `127.0.0.1:19877`, which is straightforward on the host but awkward from
   inside Docker.

4. Verify the stored identity.

   ```bash
   opencode auth list
   ```

### MCP servers

Both agents support remote MCP servers (streamable-http). On first start the
container registers a public example server, `https://jarakube.eu/mcp`
(Jaraco website content: services, blog posts, categories, Jarakube
resources), with **both** OpenCode and goose. Opt out with
`MCP_EXAMPLE_ENABLED=0`, or override name/URL via `MCP_EXAMPLE_NAME` /
`MCP_EXAMPLE_URL`.

Verify:

```bash
opencode mcp list    # shows jarakube-website (connected)
```

See [docs/mcp.md](docs/mcp.md) for adding your own servers to either agent.

### Integrating other agents

The container is a generic environment for CLI coding agents - Claude Code,
Codex CLI, and Gemini CLI install via npm and run alongside OpenCode and
goose. All of them share the same skill format (`SKILL.md` with
name/description frontmatter), so this repo's `skills/` directory maps into
each one; MCP servers are configured per agent.

See [docs/agents.md](docs/agents.md) for install commands, skills
locations, MCP config formats, derived-image recipes, and authentication
notes per agent.

### Repository notes

- [llms.txt](llms.txt) / [llms-full.txt](llms-full.txt): documentation
  index and full flattened docs for LLM consumption (per
  [llmstxt.org](https://llmstxt.org)) - regenerate both when docs change.
- Every commit must be signed off (DCO): commit with
  `git commit --signoff`, producing a `Signed-off-by: Name <email>`
  trailer matching the commit author. CI rejects unsigned commits.
- PR image builds are gated: the Build workflow only builds/pushes a PR's
  image after the repository owner comments `ready for test` on the PR.
  Pushes to `main` always build.
- Add new skills under `skills/<name>/SKILL.md`; they will be copied into the
  image on build. See [skills/README.md](skills/README.md).
- The goosetown directory is a git submodule: clone with
  `--recurse-submodules` and update with `git submodule update --remote`.
- Review any local credential or key material before publishing images or
  sharing this repository.

## File: AGENTS.md

Guidance for AI coding agents working on **this repository** (the thoth
agent container). For how the agents inside the container consume
AGENTS.md in *your* projects, see
[docs/agents.md](docs/agents.md#agentsmd-project-instructions).

### Project overview

This repository builds **thoth**, a containerized CLI agent environment:
OpenCode + goose/goosetown + kubectl, with a Prometheus metrics exporter,
a generic skill pack, and Docker Compose wiring. It is intended for
open-source publication - it must contain no private infrastructure
references. The project is maintained and supported by
[jarakube.eu](https://jarakube.eu); the example MCP server
`https://jarakube.eu/mcp` in the docs is an intentional public reference.

### Build and run

- Build requires the host user's uid/gid so bind mounts are writable:
  `make build` (= `HOST_UID=$(id -u) HOST_GID=$(id -g) docker compose build`)
- Start: `make up`; shell: `make shell`; one-shot: `make run CMD="opencode --version"`
- Plain `docker compose up` without HOST_UID/HOST_GID produces a
  uid-mismatched image; the entrypoint fails fast with a clear error if
  /workspace is not writable
- The goosetown directory is a git submodule of
  https://github.com/aaif-goose/goosetown - clone with
  `--recurse-submodules`

### Verification

Before committing changes, run what applies:

```bash
bash -n scripts/container-entrypoint.sh        # entrypoint syntax
docker compose config --quiet                  # compose validity (from repo root)
./test-dockerfile.sh                           # Dockerfile sanity checks
make build                                     # full image build (slow)
```

For behavioral changes, verify live: `make up`, then
`docker compose exec -T agent bash -c '...'` (use `-T`; exec with a TTY
can hang in some environments). Check `docker compose logs agent` for the
goosetown clone and MCP registration lines.

### Repository structure

- `Dockerfile` - image: ubuntu 26.04, kubectl 1.36, goose (ARG GOOSE_VERSION),
  opencode from npm (or `build/opencode/opencode` custom binary), goosetown
  tooling copy at `/app/goosetown`
- `scripts/container-entrypoint.sh` - startup: workspace writability check,
  goosetown clone into `$GOOSETOWN_DIR`, example MCP registration, metrics
  exporter
- `docker-compose.yml` / `Makefile` - workspace bind mount, opencode-data
  volume, uid-matched build args
- `skills/` - OpenCode skills bundled into the image; `docs/` - integration
  guides (MCP, other agents)

### Conventions

- Keep all user-generated data on the host filesystem (bind mounts), never
  in anonymous or root-chowned locations. Nothing on the host is ever
  chowned by the container.
- The example MCP server URL `https://jarakube.eu/mcp` is an intentional
  public example; other internal names must not appear anywhere.
- Before publishing or merging, scan for leaks:
  `rg -i "pdr-harbor|happy_bardeen|jarakube-jaraco" --hidden -g '!.git' .`
  Intentional public references that MAY match scans: `jarakube.eu`
  (maintainer/site/MCP example) and the Jaraco GmbH maintainer credit in
  the README. Internal infrastructure names must never appear.
- Docs changes should be verified against the official docs of the tool in
  question; agent CLI facts (flags, config formats, versions) change often.
- Commit messages: conventional style, one line summary + body paragraphs
  (`feat:`, `fix:`, `docs:`, `chore:`).
- Every commit MUST carry a `Signed-off-by: Name <email>` trailer
  (DCO, https://developercertificate.org/): commit with
  `git commit --signoff`. CI rejects unsigned commits.
- Skills use the agent-skills standard: `<name>/SKILL.md` with `name` and
  `description` frontmatter.
- After changing any documentation (README, docs/, skills/README.md),
  regenerate `llms.txt` and `llms-full.txt`: the index lists each doc
  with a one-line description; the full file concatenates all docs under
  `## File: <path>` markers (drop each file's H1, demote other headings
  by one level, never touch fenced code blocks). Keep both in sync with
  the docs or the check
  `rg -c '^## File: ' llms-full.txt` (must equal the doc count) fails.

## File: skills/README.md

This directory contains [OpenCode](https://opencode.ai) skills that are copied
into the container image at build time.

```
skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md   ->  /home/appuser/.config/opencode/skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md
```

The `Dockerfile` bundles everything under `skills/` into
`/home/appuser/.config/opencode/skills/`, which is OpenCode's global skill
location for the in-container `appuser`.

### What ships in the image

| Skill | Purpose |
|-------|---------|
| `ceph` | Production-oriented Ceph expert persona: RADOS, RGW, dynamic bucket sharding, Rook on Kubernetes, OpenStack integration |

The `ceph` skill is intentionally generic: it demonstrates the expected
`SKILL.md` format (YAML frontmatter with `name` and `description`, followed by
markdown instructions) without referencing any private infrastructure.

### Adding your own skills

1. Create `skills/<your-skill>/SKILL.md`:

   ```markdown
   ---
   name: my-skill
   description: One-line description of when to use this skill.
   ---

   # My Skill

   Instructions for the agent ...
   ```

2. Rebuild the image:

   ```bash
   docker build -t thoth .
   ```

3. Verify inside the container:

   ```bash
   docker run --rm -it agent bash -c 'ls ~/.config/opencode/skills/'
   ```

### Mapping skills into the container without rebuilding

Build-time bundling is convenient but not the only option. Any of the
following work at runtime, with no image rebuild:

| Method | How | Best for |
|--------|-----|----------|
| **Bind mount** (recommended) | `docker run -v "$(pwd)/my-skills:/home/appuser/.config/opencode/skills:ro" ...` | Development: edit skills on the host, reload instantly |
| **Volume** | `docker volume create agent-skills` then mount it at `/home/appuser/.config/opencode/skills` | Long-lived skill collections shared across containers |
| **Kubernetes ConfigMap** | Mount a ConfigMap at `/home/appuser/.config/opencode/skills` (or use ` projected volumes` to combine ConfigMap + image content) | Cluster deployments; version skills via GitOps |
| **Kubernetes PVC** | Persistent volume mounted at the same path | Large skill packs or skills generated at runtime |
| **`docker cp`** | `docker cp my-skill running-container:/home/appuser/.config/opencode/skills/` | Quick experimentation in a running container |
| **Custom `FROM` image** | `FROM thoth:latest` + `COPY my-skills/ /home/appuser/.config/opencode/skills/` | Derived, opinionated images that bake in your skills |
| **Git clone at startup** | Mount a script/entrypoint hook that clones your skills repo into the skills dir | Keeping skills in their own repository with independent versioning |

#### Notes on Kubernetes mounts

When you mount a ConfigMap or volume over `/home/appuser/.config/opencode/skills`,
it **shadows** the image-bundled skills. To combine both, use a `projected`
volume:

```yaml
volumes:
  - name: skills
    projected:
      sources:
        - configMap:
            name: my-extra-skills
      # image-bundled skills are not directly projectable; for combined
      # setups, copy the bundled skills into the ConfigMap or use an init
      # container that merges them into an emptyDir.
```

A common pattern for merging image skills with dynamic skills:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: agent
    volumeMounts:
      - name: merged-skills
        mountPath: /home/appuser/.config/opencode/skills
initContainers:
  - name: copy-bundled-skills
    image: agent:latest
    command: ["cp", "-r", "/home/appuser/.config/opencode/skills/.", "/skills/"]
    volumeMounts:
      - name: merged-skills
        mountPath: /skills
```

(Add a second init container or projected source that also writes your
dynamic skills into `merged-skills`.)

### Keeping private skills out of the open-source image

If you maintain organization-specific skills (internal tooling, private
repositories, customer systems), keep them in a separate private repository and
map them into the container at runtime using one of the methods above. Never
add them to this repository's `skills/` directory - the build copies everything
it finds there into the public image.

A typical split:

- **Public repo (this one)**: generic skills (`ceph`), image, scripts, docs.
- **Private repo (yours)**: `skills/<org-skill>/SKILL.md` + supporting files,
  mounted at runtime or baked into a private `FROM`-derived image.

## File: docs/mcp.md

Both agents in this container support remote MCP servers over the
streamable-http transport:

- **OpenCode**: `opencode mcp add <name> --url <url>` (stored in the OpenCode
  config, e.g. `~/.config/opencode/opencode.jsonc`)
- **Goose**: `mcp_servers` in `~/.config/goose/config.yaml` (or
  `goose configure` → Add Extension → Remote Extension (Streamable HTTP))

### Example: the Jarakube website MCP server

The container entrypoint registers a public example MCP server for both
agents on first start (opt-out via `MCP_EXAMPLE_ENABLED=0`):

```
https://jarakube.eu/mcp
```

It is operated by [jarakube.eu](https://jarakube.eu), the sovereign
Kubernetes platform that also maintains and supports this project, and
serves the Jaraco GmbH website content: services, blog posts, categories,
and Jarakube platform resources, plus a `draft_email` tool. It requires no
authentication.

#### What gets configured

OpenCode (via `opencode mcp add`):

```bash
opencode mcp add jarakube-website --url https://jarakube.eu/mcp
```

Goose (`~/.config/goose/config.yaml`):

```yaml
mcp_servers:
  jarakube-website:
    url: https://jarakube.eu/mcp
```

#### Verify

```bash
# OpenCode: list configured MCP servers and their status
opencode mcp list

# Goose: check the extension is loaded (requires a configured provider)
goose doctor
```

Then ask either agent something like "list the available Jarakube website
resources" - the MCP tools/resources appear alongside the built-in tools.

### Adding your own MCP servers

#### OpenCode

```bash
# remote server
opencode mcp add my-server --url https://mcp.example.com

# remote server with auth header
opencode mcp add my-server --url https://mcp.example.com \
  --header "Authorization=Bearer $MY_TOKEN"

# local stdio server
opencode mcp add my-server --env KEY=value -- my-command arg1
```

#### Goose

```yaml
# ~/.config/goose/config.yaml
mcp_servers:
  my-server:
    url: https://mcp.example.com
    # auth:
    #   type: bearer   # token from keyring/env
```

Or interactively: `goose configure` → Add Extension → Remote Extension
(Streamable HTTP).

### Environment variables

| Variable | Purpose | Default |
|----------|---------|---------|
| `MCP_EXAMPLE_ENABLED` | Set `0` to skip registering the example server | `1` |
| `MCP_EXAMPLE_NAME` | Name used for the example server registration | `jarakube-website` |
| `MCP_EXAMPLE_URL` | URL of the example server | `https://jarakube.eu/mcp` |

## File: docs/agents.md

This container ships OpenCode and goose/goosetown, but it is a generic
tooling environment: any CLI coding agent that runs on Linux and installs
via npm (or a plain binary) works inside it. This guide shows how to add
the common agents, where each one loads skills and MCP servers from, and
how to map your existing `skills/` directory into them.

The general pattern for every agent:

1. Install it in the running container (or bake it into a derived image).
   Global npm installs need root: `docker compose exec -u root thoth npm i -g <pkg>` (or `make shell`, then `sudo`-style `-u root` exec). The container user `appuser` cannot write `/usr/local/lib/node_modules`.
2. Point its skills directory at your skills (bind mount, symlink, or
   copy - see [skills/README.md](../skills/README.md) for the same mapping
   techniques used for OpenCode).
3. Register MCP servers in its config (the example
   [jarakube.eu/mcp](mcp.md) server works with every agent below).
4. Add an `AGENTS.md` to your project so every agent picks up the same
   build/test instructions (see below).

### AGENTS.md (project instructions)

[AGENTS.md](https://agents.md) is the open "README for agents" format:
an `AGENTS.md` file at the repository root gives coding agents build and
test commands, conventions, and project context. This repo ships one
(see [AGENTS.md](../AGENTS.md)); agents working *in your workspace* read
yours the same way.

Each agent loads it as follows:

| Agent | AGENTS.md support |
|---|---|
| OpenCode | Native: project `AGENTS.md` (plus global `~/.config/opencode/AGENTS.md`); `/init` scaffolds one. Falls back to `CLAUDE.md` if no `AGENTS.md` exists |
| Codex CLI | Native: reads `AGENTS.md` from the working directory up to the repo root (nested files supported; nearest wins) |
| Claude Code | Reads `AGENTS.md` when no `CLAUDE.md`/`CLAUDE.local.md` exists in or above the working directory (v2.1.277+); otherwise import it from `CLAUDE.md` with `@AGENTS.md`, or change the Project instructions setting |
| Gemini CLI | Via config: `{"context": {"fileName": "AGENTS.md"}}` in `~/.gemini/settings.json` (default file is `GEMINI.md`) |
| goose | Reads instructions from the goosetown clone's `AGENTS.md` (orchestrator/delegate context) |

Practical tips:

- One repo-level `AGENTS.md` covers OpenCode, Codex, and (with the
  fallback rule) Claude Code - no per-agent files needed.
- For Claude Code with an existing `CLAUDE.md`, add an import line so
  both stay in sync: `See @AGENTS.md for build and test instructions.`
- Large monorepos: nested `AGENTS.md` files per package; agents read the
  nearest one.

### Quick reference

| Agent | Install | Skills location | MCP config |
|---|---|---|---|
| [OpenCode](https://opencode.ai) | `npm i -g opencode-ai` | `~/.config/opencode/skills/` | `opencode mcp add` |
| [Claude Code](https://code.claude.com/docs) | `npm i -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code` | `~/.claude/skills/` (personal), `.claude/skills/` (project) | `claude mcp add --transport http <name> <url>` |
| [Codex CLI](https://developers.openai.com/codex) | `npm i -g @openai/codex` | `~/.agents/skills/` (user), `.agents/skills/` (repo), `/etc/codex/skills` (admin) | `codex mcp add` / `~/.codex/config.toml` |
| [Gemini CLI](https://geminicli.com/docs) | `npm i -g @google/gemini-cli` | `~/.gemini/skills` | `~/.gemini/settings.json` (`mcpServers`) |
| [goose](https://github.com/aaif-goose/goose) | preinstalled | goosetown skills (see [goosetown](#goose--goosetown-preinstalled)) | `~/.config/goose/config.yaml` (`mcp_servers`) |

All skill formats above use the same core convention: a directory per
skill containing a `SKILL.md` with `name` and `description` frontmatter
(the [agent skills standard](https://agentskills.io)). A skill written
once in this repo's `skills/` format works for OpenCode, Claude Code,
Codex, and Gemini CLI - only the directory it lives in differs.

### Claude Code

Install and verify:

```bash
# as root (appuser cannot write /usr/local/lib/node_modules)
docker compose exec -u root thoth npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code

# as appuser
docker compose exec thoth claude --version
docker compose exec thoth claude /login     # authenticate (Anthropic account or API key)
```

(Verified with Claude Code 2.1.322 in this container.)

#### Skills

Claude Code loads personal skills from `~/.claude/skills/` and project
skills from `.claude/skills/` in the working directory. To reuse this
repo's skills:

```bash
# personal skills for all projects
mkdir -p ~/.claude/skills
cp -r /path/to/repo/skills/* ~/.claude/skills/

# or per-project, versioned in git
mkdir -p .claude/skills
cp -r /path/to/repo/skills/ceph .claude/skills/
```

Or bind-mount them at runtime (host paths, no copy):

```bash
docker compose run --rm thoth bash -c '
  mkdir -p ~/.claude/skills
  cp -r /workspace/.claude-shared/skills/* ~/.claude/skills/ 2>/dev/null || true
  claude'
```

#### MCP servers

```bash
# remote streamable-http server (the example from docs/mcp.md)
claude mcp add --transport http jarakube-website https://jarakube.eu/mcp

# with an auth header
claude mcp add --transport http my-server https://mcp.example.com \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer $MY_TOKEN"

# local stdio server
claude mcp add --env API_KEY=xxx --transport stdio my-tool -- npx -y some-mcp-server

claude mcp list    # verify
```

Config lives in `~/.claude.json` (local scope by default; `--scope user`
for all projects, `--scope project` writes `.mcp.json`).

### Codex CLI

Install and verify (global install needs root, see above):

```bash
docker compose exec -u root thoth npm install -g @openai/codex
docker compose exec thoth codex --version
docker compose exec thoth codex login      # ChatGPT account or API key
```

#### Skills

Codex scans (closest first, all loaded in parallel):

- `$CWD/.agents/skills` and parents up to the repo root (repo scope)
- `~/.agents/skills` (user scope - applies to every project)
- `/etc/codex/skills` (admin scope - useful for baking skills into
  derived container images)

```bash
# user-scope skills
mkdir -p ~/.agents/skills
cp -r /path/to/repo/skills/* ~/.agents/skills/

# admin scope inside a derived image (Dockerfile):
# COPY skills/ /etc/codex/skills/
```

#### MCP servers

```bash
# stdio server
codex mcp add my-tool -- npx -y some-mcp-server

# verify
codex mcp list
```

Remote (streamable-http) servers go in `~/.codex/config.toml`:

```toml
[mcp_servers.jarakube-website]
url = "https://jarakube.eu/mcp"
```

### Gemini CLI

Install and verify (global install needs root, see above):

```bash
docker compose exec -u root thoth npm install -g @google/gemini-cli
docker compose exec thoth gemini --version
docker compose exec thoth gemini           # OAuth login on first start, or export GEMINI_API_KEY
```

Note: since June 2026 Google points free-tier / Google AI accounts at the
Antigravity CLI; `@google/gemini-cli` remains the open-source CLI for
Gemini Code Assist (Standard/Enterprise) and API-key/Vertex usage.

#### Skills

Gemini CLI loads skills from `~/.gemini/skills` (user) and a `.gemini/skills`
directory in the project. Same `SKILL.md` convention:

```bash
mkdir -p ~/.gemini/skills
cp -r /path/to/repo/skills/* ~/.gemini/skills/
```

#### MCP servers

`~/.gemini/settings.json`:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "jarakube-website": {
      "httpUrl": "https://jarakube.eu/mcp"
    }
  }
}
```

(`url` is the SSE transport key; `httpUrl` is streamable-http. Recent
versions also have `gemini mcp add`.) Verify with `/mcp` inside a session.

### goose / goosetown (preinstalled)

goose is already installed; goosetown is cloned into the workspace at
`$GOOSETOWN_DIR` (default `/workspace/goosetown`) on first start, and all
goosetown env points there. Its skills live in the clone (goosetown uses
`.claude/skills/` inside its repo for its orchestrator/delegate skills).

Add remote MCP servers to `~/.config/goose/config.yaml`:

```yaml
mcp_servers:
  jarakube-website:
    url: https://jarakube.eu/mcp
```

(The container entrypoint writes this example server automatically - see
[docs/mcp.md](mcp.md).)

### Baking agents into a derived image

For repeatable setups, extend the image instead of installing ad hoc:

```dockerfile
FROM thoth:latest

# extra agents
RUN npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code @openai/codex @google/gemini-cli

# skills shared by all agents (Codex admin scope; symlink for the others)
COPY skills/ /etc/codex/skills/
RUN mkdir -p /home/appuser/.claude/skills /home/appuser/.agents/skills \
    && ln -sf /etc/codex/skills/* /home/appuser/.claude/skills/ \
    && ln -sf /etc/codex/skills/* /home/appuser/.agents/skills/

# pre-register MCP servers
RUN printf 'mcp_servers:\n  jarakube-website:\n    url: https://jarakube.eu/mcp\n' \
    > /home/appuser/.config/goose/config.yaml
```

Build and run:

```bash
docker build -t my-agent-stack .
docker run --rm -it -v "$(pwd)/workspace:/workspace" my-agent-stack
```

### Authentication notes

- Each agent authenticates independently (OAuth login or API key env
  vars: `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `OPENAI_API_KEY`, `GEMINI_API_KEY`, ...).
- OAuth callbacks bind to `localhost` on the host; inside the container
  use API-key auth, or authenticate on the host and mount the agent's
  credentials (the same pattern the README shows for OpenCode's
  `auth.json`).
- Agent credentials live under each agent's home directory
  (`~/.claude`, `~/.codex`, `~/.gemini`). To persist them across
  container restarts, add a compose volume for `~/.agents-credentials`
  style state or mount the whole `~/.config`/dotfiles tree.

## File: LITELLM_CONFIGURATION.md

This document explains how to configure the agents in this container to use
**LiteLLM** as the LLM provider.

### Overview

[LiteLLM](https://litellm.ai/) is a proxy server that allows you to use 100+ LLMs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Mistral, Local models via Ollama, etc.) with a unified OpenAI-compatible API. Since LiteLLM speaks the OpenAI API format, agents connect to it the same way they connect to any OpenAI-compatible endpoint - there is no "litellm" provider type in either OpenCode or goose.

- **goose**: configured via the LiteLLM config file and the `goose-litellm`
  wrapper described below.
- **OpenCode**: configured as a custom provider using the
  `openai-compatible` runtime package - see
  [Using LiteLLM with OpenCode](#using-litellm-with-opencode) below.

### Keeping both in sync

Both agents need the same data (endpoint URL, API key, model list), so
this container configures them from a **single source of truth**: the
`LLM_*` environment variables. `scripts/sync-llm-config.sh` runs at
container start and writes both configs:

| Source of truth (env) | OpenCode (generated) | goose (generated) |
|---|---|---|
| `LLM_ENDPOINT` (incl. `/v1`) | `provider.litellm.options.baseURL` in `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json` | `LITELLM_HOST` + `LITELLM_BASE_PATH` in `~/.config/goose/set-env.sh` |
| `LLM_API_KEY_ENV` (default `CUSTOM_LITELLM_API_KEY`) | `provider.litellm.options.apiKey` (`{env:...}` reference) | `LITELLM_API_KEY` (same env reference) |
| `LLM_MODELS` | `provider.litellm.models` map | `GOOSE_MODEL` default (first entry) |
| `LLM_DEFAULT_MODEL` (default: first of `LLM_MODELS`) | top-level `model` (`litellm/<id>`, only when unset) | `GOOSE_MODEL` in `config.yaml` |

The script also sets `GOOSE_PROVIDER: litellm` in
`~/.config/goose/config.yaml` (using goose's built-in litellm provider)
unless a provider is already configured, and hooks the generated env into
`~/.bashrc` so interactive shells see it.

Behavior:

- Unset `LLM_ENDPOINT` → no-op; both agents fall back to their own
  configuration (goose via `goose-litellm`, OpenCode via `/connect`).
- Re-running is safe: OpenCode's `provider.litellm` entry is regenerated
  (user's other config keys preserved), goose's `GOOSE_MODEL` updated in
  place.
- After changing `LLM_*` in `.env`, restart the container
  (`docker compose up -d`) to re-run the sync.

#### API key resolution (pass / secrets)

The key is resolved in this order (first hit wins):

1. The env var named by `LLM_API_KEY_ENV` (e.g. `CUSTOM_LITELLM_API_KEY`)
2. The docker compose secret file `/run/secrets/llm_api_key` - mounted
   from `LLM_API_KEY_FILE` on the host

For `pass` users, `make up` handles this automatically: it runs
`pass show $PASS_LLM_ENTRY` (default entry `llm/thoth-api-key`), writes
the first line to a temporary mode-600 file, exports it as
`LLM_API_KEY_FILE` for the compose secret, and removes the file when
done. The key therefore exists only in the pass store, the short-lived
temp file, and the container's secret mount - never in `.env`, the
compose file, the image, or any generated config (both configs reference
the env var, they never embed the key).

### What's Included (goose)

The Dockerfile includes:

1. **LiteLLM Configuration File** (`/home/appuser/.config/goose/litellm-config.yaml`)
   - Pre-configured models for Mistral (default), OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google
   - Environment variable placeholders for API keys
   - Default fallback models

2. **Wrapper Script** (`/usr/local/bin/goose-litellm`)
   - Automatically sets up environment for LiteLLM
   - Provides goose with LiteLLM support
   - Easy to use command: `goose-litellm`

3. **Environment Variables**
   - `GOOSE_LLM_PROVIDER` - Set the LLM provider (e.g., "mistral", "openai", "anthropic")
   - `GOOSE_LLM_MODEL` - Set the specific model to use
   - Standard API key environment variables for each provider

### Supported Providers

The configuration includes support for:

| Provider | Models | Environment Variable |
|----------|--------|---------------------|
| **OpenAI** | gpt-4, gpt-3.5-turbo | `OPENAI_API_KEY` |
| **Anthropic** | claude-3-opus, claude-3-sonnet | `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` |
| **Google** | gemini-pro | `GEMINI_API_KEY` |
| **Mistral** | mistral-small, mistral-large | `MISTRAL_API_KEY` |
| **Ollama** | llama3, other local models | `OLLAMA_API_BASE` |

### Quick Start

`CUSTOM_LITELLM_API_KEY` is required and must be set before using the LiteLLM-backed Goose commands.

#### Method 1: Using Environment Variables (Recommended)

```bash
# Required for LiteLLM access
export CUSTOM_LITELLM_API_KEY="your-litellm-key"

# Set your API keys
export OPENAI_API_KEY="your-openai-key"
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="your-anthropic-key"

# Choose provider and model
export GOOSE_LLM_PROVIDER="openai"
export GOOSE_LLM_MODEL="gpt-4"

# Run goose with LiteLLM support
goose-litellm session "Analyze this codebase"
```

#### Method 2: Using the Wrapper Script

```bash
# Run goose with default LiteLLM configuration
goose-litellm session "Help me debug this Python code"
```

#### Method 3: Direct goose Usage

```bash
# Set environment variables
export OPENAI_API_KEY="your-key"

# Run goose directly (it will use LiteLLM if configured)
goose session "Review my Dockerfile"
```

### Configuration Files

#### LiteLLM Config File
Location: `/home/appuser/.config/goose/litellm-config.yaml`

This file contains:
- Model definitions with provider-specific parameters
- Environment variable placeholders for API keys
- Default settings for LiteLLM

You can customize this file to add more models or change settings.

#### Environment Setup
Location: `/home/appuser/.config/goose/set-env.sh` (created when you run the config script)

This script sets up environment variables based on your API keys.

### Advanced Configuration

#### Adding Custom Models

Edit `/home/appuser/.config/goose/litellm-config.yaml`:

```yaml
model_list:
  - model_name: "my-custom-model"
    litellm_params:
      model: "custom-provider/custom-model-name"
      api_key: "${CUSTOM_API_KEY:-}"
      api_base: "${CUSTOM_API_BASE:-https://api.custom.com/v1}"
      other_param: "value"
```

#### Using Local Models (Ollama)

```bash
# Start Ollama
docker run -d -p 11434:11434 --name ollama ollama/ollama

# Pull a model
curl -X POST http://localhost:11434/api/pull -d '{"name": "llama3"}'

# Set environment variables
export OLLAMA_API_BASE="http://localhost:11434"

# Configure goose to use local model
export GOOSE_LLM_PROVIDER="ollama"
export GOOSE_LLM_MODEL="llama3"

goose-litellm session "Explain this code"
```

#### Multiple Providers with Fallback

LiteLLM supports routing strategies and fallback models. You can configure this in the YAML file:

```yaml
general_settings:
  default_fallback_models:
    - "mistral-large"
    - "mistral-small"

router_settings:
  routing_strategy: "usage-based"
  enable_tag_filtering: true
```

### Environment Variables Reference

#### Provider-Specific Variables

| Provider | API Key Variable | Model Variable | API Base Variable |
|----------|------------------|----------------|-------------------|
| OpenAI | `OPENAI_API_KEY` | `OPENAI_MODEL` | `OPENAI_API_BASE` |
| Anthropic | `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` | `ANTHROPIC_MODEL` | N/A |
| Google | `GEMINI_API_KEY` | `GEMINI_MODEL` | N/A |
| Mistral | `MISTRAL_API_KEY` | `MISTRAL_MODEL` | N/A |
| Ollama | N/A | `OLLAMA_MODEL` | `OLLAMA_API_BASE` |

#### Goose-Specific Variables

| Variable | Description | Default Value |
|----------|-------------|---------------|
| `GOOSE_LLM_PROVIDER` | LLM provider to use | `mistral` |
| `GOOSE_LLM_MODEL` | Specific model to use | `mistral-small-latest` |
| `LITELLM_CONFIG_FILE` | Path to LiteLLM config | `/home/appuser/.config/goose/litellm-config.yaml` |

#### LiteLLM-Specific Variables

| Variable | Description | Default Value |
|----------|-------------|---------------|
| `CUSTOM_LITELLM_API_KEY` | Required API key for LiteLLM access | (required) |
| `LITELLM_MASTER_KEY` | Master key for LiteLLM | (empty) |
| `LITELLM_DATABASE_URL` | Database connection string | `sqlite:///./litellm.db` |
| `REDIS_URL` | Redis connection string | (empty) |

### Troubleshooting

#### Issue: "Model not found"

**Solution**: Make sure the model name in your environment variable matches one of the configured models in the YAML file.

```bash
# Wrong
export GOOSE_LLM_MODEL="gpt-4o"

# Correct
export GOOSE_LLM_MODEL="gpt-4"
```

#### Issue: "API key not set"

**Solution**: Export `CUSTOM_LITELLM_API_KEY` and the required provider API key environment variable.

```bash
# Required for LiteLLM
export CUSTOM_LITELLM_API_KEY="your-litellm-key"

# For OpenAI
export OPENAI_API_KEY="sk-..."

# For Anthropic
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="sk-ant-..."
```

#### Issue: "LiteLLM not working"

**Solution**: Verify that goose is installed and the wrapper script exists:

```bash
ls -la /usr/local/bin/goose-litellm
which goose
```

#### Issue: "Connection refused"

**Solution**: Check that your API base URL is correct:

```bash
# For custom providers
export OPENAI_API_BASE="https://api.openai.com/v1"
```

### Examples

#### Example 1: Using OpenAI GPT-4

```bash
# Set API key
export OPENAI_API_KEY="sk-your-openai-key-here"

# Configure goose
export GOOSE_LLM_PROVIDER="openai"
export GOOSE_LLM_MODEL="gpt-4"

# Run goose
goose-litellm session "Review this Kubernetes deployment YAML"
```

#### Example 2: Using Anthropic Claude 3 Opus

```bash
# Set API key
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="sk-ant-your-anthropic-key-here"

# Configure goose
export GOOSE_LLM_PROVIDER="anthropic"
export GOOSE_LLM_MODEL="claude-3-opus"

# Run goose
goose-litellm session "Explain this complex algorithm"
```

#### Example 3: Using Local Ollama Model

```bash
# Start Ollama (if not running)
docker run -d -p 11434:11434 --name ollama ollama/ollama

# Pull a model
curl -X POST http://localhost:11434/api/pull -d '{"name": "llama3"}'

# Configure goose
export GOOSE_LLM_PROVIDER="ollama"
export GOOSE_LLM_MODEL="llama3"

# Run goose
goose-litellm session "Help me understand this Python code"
```

#### Example 4: Multi-Provider with Fallback

```bash
# Set multiple API keys
export OPENAI_API_KEY="sk-..."
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="sk-ant-..."
export GEMINI_API_KEY="..."

# Configure LiteLLM config for fallback
export GOOSE_LLM_PROVIDER="mistral"

# Run goose - it will use the best available model
goose-litellm session "Analyze this entire codebase"
```

### Performance Tips

1. **Use smaller models** for quick tasks (mistral-small, gpt-3.5-turbo)
2. **Use larger models** for complex analysis (claude-3-opus, gpt-4)
3. **Set up caching** with LiteLLM to reduce API costs
4. **Use local models** for privacy-sensitive code
5. **Monitor usage** with LiteLLM's built-in dashboard

### Security Considerations

✅ **Secure by default**:
- API keys are not hardcoded in the container
- Keys are passed via environment variables
- Configuration files are owned by appuser
- No sensitive data is stored in the image

🔒 **Best Practices**:
- Use Kubernetes secrets or Docker secrets for production
- Rotate API keys regularly
- Use different keys for different environments
- Never commit API keys to version control

### Integration with Goosetown

When using goose with goosetown, the LiteLLM configuration works seamlessly:

```bash
# Start goosetown orchestrator
goose load source:goosetown-orchestrator

# Configure goose first
export OPENAI_API_KEY="your-key"
export GOOSE_LLM_PROVIDER="openai"

# Then agents will use LiteLLM automatically
```

### Using LiteLLM with OpenCode

OpenCode has no native "litellm" provider - and it does not need one.
LiteLLM exposes an OpenAI-compatible API, so OpenCode connects to it as a
custom provider using the `@ai-sdk/openai-compatible` package.

Add this to `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json` (global) or `opencode.json`
in your project:

```json
{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "model": "litellm/mistral-small-latest",
  "provider": {
    "litellm": {
      "npm": "@ai-sdk/openai-compatible",
      "name": "LiteLLM Proxy",
      "options": {
        "baseURL": "http://litellm-proxy:4000/v1",
        "apiKey": "{env:CUSTOM_LITELLM_API_KEY}"
      },
      "models": {
        "mistral-small-latest": { "name": "Mistral Small (via LiteLLM)" },
        "mistral-large-latest": { "name": "Mistral Large (via LiteLLM)" }
      }
    }
  }
}
```

Notes:

- `npm` selects the OpenAI-compatible runtime package; LiteLLM speaks the
  OpenAI API format, so no litellm-specific package is needed.
- `options.apiKey` reads the credential from the `CUSTOM_LITELLM_API_KEY`
  environment variable via the `{env:...}` placeholder (this container's
  compose setup passes that variable). Alternatively run `/connect` and
  pick the `litellm` provider to store the key in `auth.json`.
- `options.baseURL` must point at the LiteLLM proxy's `/v1` endpoint.
  Adjust the host to wherever your proxy runs (`http://localhost:4000/v1`
  when the proxy runs on the same machine, `http://host.docker.internal:4000/v1`
  from inside a container, a service name on a Docker network, etc.).
- Each key under `models` must match an ID the proxy's `GET /v1/models`
  returns; the reference format is `litellm/<model-id>`
  (e.g. `litellm/mistral-small-latest`).

Verify inside the container:

```bash
opencode models litellm
opencode run --model litellm/mistral-small-latest "Reply with OK"
```

(Verified with OpenCode 1.19.5: the provider appears in
`opencode models litellm` and requests route to the configured baseURL.)

> **OpenCode V2**: if you upgrade to OpenCode V2, the config schema
> changes to `providers` (plural) with a `package` field instead of
> `npm`:
>
> ```jsonc
> {
>   "providers": {
>     "litellm": {
>       "name": "LiteLLM Proxy",
>       "env": ["CUSTOM_LITELLM_API_KEY"],
>       "package": "@opencode/ai/providers/openai-compatible",
>       "settings": { "baseURL": "http://litellm-proxy:4000/v1" },
>       "models": { "mistral-small-latest": { "name": "Mistral Small (via LiteLLM)" } }
>     }
>   }
> }
> ```

### Documentation References

- [LiteLLM Official Documentation](https://docs.litellm.ai/)
- [Goose Documentation](https://goose-docs.ai/)
- [Goose GitHub Repository](https://github.com/aaif-goose/goose)
- [LiteLLM GitHub Repository](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm)
- [OpenCode Providers Documentation](https://opencode.ai/docs/providers/) (custom providers / `openai-compatible` package)

### Support

If you encounter issues with LiteLLM configuration:

1. Check the LiteLLM logs: `docker logs litellm`
2. Verify API keys are correct
3. Test LiteLLM directly: `curl http://localhost:4000/chat/completions`
4. Check goose configuration: `goose doctor`

**Status**: ✅ **COMPLETE**
**Date**: 2026-09-04
**Configuration**: Ready for use with all major LLM providers

## File: GOOSETOWN_INTEGRATION.md

This document describes the changes made to integrate goose and goosetown into the coding agent container.

### Changes Made

#### 1. Updated Dockerfile

The main Dockerfile (`Dockerfile`) has been updated to include goose and goosetown support.

##### Added Dependencies:
- `python3-yaml` - Required by goosetown
- `pipx` - For Python package management
- `wget` - For downloading goose binary
- `unzip` - For extracting packages

##### Added goose Binary Installation:
```dockerfile
# Current Dockerfile installs goose via scripts/install-goose.sh from the
# GitHub releases (asset naming: goose-<arch>-unknown-linux-gnu.tar.bz2):
# https://github.com/aaif-goose/goose/releases
ARG GOOSE_VERSION=v1.50.0
COPY --chmod=755 scripts/install-goose.sh /usr/local/bin/install-goose.sh
RUN GOOSE_VERSION=${GOOSE_VERSION} GOOSE_BIN_DIR=/usr/local/bin \
    /usr/local/bin/install-goose.sh && /usr/local/bin/goose --version
```

##### Added goosetown Directory:
```dockerfile
# Install goosetown
RUN mkdir -p /app/goosetown
COPY goosetown/ /app/goosetown/
```

##### Added goosetown Scripts for appuser:
```dockerfile
# Copy goosetown scripts for appuser
COPY --chown=appuser:appuser goosetown/goose_gui /usr/local/bin/goose_gui
COPY --chown=appuser:appuser goosetown/gtwall /usr/local/bin/gtwall
COPY --chown=appuser:appuser goosetown/dashboard /usr/local/bin/goosetown-dashboard
```

##### Added Environment Setup:
```dockerfile
# NOTE: GOOSETOWN_DIR is set by the container entrypoint, which clones a
# goosetown working repository into the workspace and points GOOSETOWN_DIR
# (plus GUIDES_DIR/PLANS_DIR/RESEARCH_DIR/WORK_LOGS_DIR) at it. The image
# copy at /app/goosetown is a tooling fallback only.
RUN echo 'export PATH="/usr/local/bin:$PATH"' >> /home/appuser/.bashrc
```

##### Updated File Permissions:
```dockerfile
RUN chown -R appuser:appuser /home/appuser/.local /home/appuser/.ssh /home/appuser/.config /app/goosetown /app/scripts
```

### What This Enables

With these changes, the coding agent container now includes:

1. **goose CLI** - The AI agent framework from the [Agentic AI Foundation](https://github.com/aaif-goose/goose)
   - Available at `/usr/local/bin/goose`
   - Can be invoked directly or via the entrypoint

2. **goosetown** - The multi-agent coordination framework
   - Located at `/app/goosetown`
   - Includes all goosetown scripts (goose, goose_gui, gtwall, dashboard)
   - Environment variables are set for easy access

3. **Telepathy Support** - Enables orchestrator → delegate communication
   - The goose wrapper creates telepathy files for session-based communication
   - Wall files for inter-agent communication

### Usage Examples

#### Running goose directly:
```bash
./goose session
```

#### Running goosetown orchestrator:
```bash
./goose load source:goosetown-orchestrator
```

#### Using gtwall for communication:
```bash
./gtwall --usage
```

### Backward Compatibility

The changes maintain backward compatibility:
- The default CMD is still `opencode`
- The entrypoint script remains unchanged
- Existing workflows continue to work
- New functionality is additive only

### Testing

To test the integration:

1. Build the container:
   ```bash
   docker build -t thoth .
   ```

2. Run the container:
   ```bash
   docker run -it thoth bash
   ```

3. Verify goose is available:
   ```bash
   goose --version
   ```

4. Verify goosetown files are present:
   ```bash
   ls -la /app/goosetown/
   ```

5. Test telepathy:
   ```bash
   ./goose doctor
   ```

### Notes

- The goose binary is downloaded from GitHub releases (v1.25.0)
- goosetown is copied from the local directory structure
- Python dependencies for goosetown can be installed using pipx by users as needed
- The integration follows the existing container structure and patterns
